newsitem.title: UK: Bundesbank warns against budget "tricks" ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank warns against budget "tricks" ahead of EMU.

text.p: A senior German central banker urged France and Italy on Tuesday not to resort to budgetary "tricks" to ensure they qualify for a single European currency.

Reimut Jochimsen, a member of the Bundesbank's policy-making council, also told journalists in London that he saw no need for a further cut in Germany's historically low interest rates, but added: "Never say never."

Jochimsen was asked about measures by France and Italy to reduce their budget deficits to bring them close to the target of no more than three percent of gross domestic product laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.

France will use a special transfer from France Telecom to cover future pension liabilities to cut its deficit next year, while Italy's 1997 budget will include a one-off "tax on Europe" to ensure the country meets the criteria.

"Even if these tricks are legal in terms of national accounting standards as defined by the European Commission ... they will not be legitimate in the sense that they are violating the spirit of what you are trying to get at," Jochimsen said.
Asked about France in particular, Jochimsen said: "It may be legal ... but I think it is illegitimate with regard to the Treaty purpose and the Treaty provisions."
As for Italy, he said it was not yet possible to evaluate its plans, but it was important that action to curb budget deficits should be durable and sustainable.
"A one-off contribution in certain calendar years does not yet provide the necessary background," Jochimsen added.

The central banker, who was speaking English, declined to comment on whether he thought European economic and monetary union (EMU) would start as planned in 1999 or which countries would join in the first wave.

But he repeated that the independent Bundesbank's long-held view that there must be no watering-down of convergence criteria on budget deficits, government debt, interest rates and exchange rates which countries must meet to participate.

"The convergence criteria are not just some whimsical torture instruments thought up by someone who would like to keep the numbers clean and pure," he said. "The threat arises that you fudge, that you do tricks. I warn against this very strongly."

Jochimsen also stressed the need for a "stability pact" to ensure EMU countries continued to pursue sound economic policies in the long term rather than viewing them as a once-off entry qualification.

Asked whether he saw scope for further cuts in German interest rates, he noted that economic conditions were improving and both short and long term interest rates were historically low, and added: "I don't see the need".
Monetary policy-makers had done their job and it was now up to the Bonn government to help stimulate growth through measures such as tax and pension reforms.
But in classic Bundesbank fashion, Jochimsen immediately sought to soften his remarks on interest rates by adding: "You never can tell. Never say never."
